title: Address and Byte Offset Explorer
description: A memory strip of eight four-byte float slots with an interactive calculator that converts an element index into a byte offset, a full address, and the VLDR instruction it produces.
creator: Real-Time DSP on a $5 Microcontroller
author: Dan McCreary
subject: Digital Signal Processing
Assembly Language
Computer Architecture
chapter_title: Talking to the FPU: Floating-Point Assembly

educational.topic: Converting an array index into a byte offset for a floating-point load
learningObjectives: Apply the formula offset = index x bytes per element
Write the VLDR instruction that loads a chosen array element
Recognize a misaligned or out-of-range byte offset
prerequisites: An array is a contiguous block of memory

controls.label: Element index
controls.purpose: Select which array element to address

controls.label: Memory slot
controls.purpose: Select an element directly from the strip

controls.label: Check offset #
controls.purpose: Test an arbitrary byte offset for alignment and range

simulationModel.modelType: Address arithmetic calculator over a fixed eight-element float array
assumptions: Elements are 32-bit floats, so the stride is exactly four bytes
The base address 0x20001000 lies in SRAM and is itself four-byte aligned
limitations: Only immediate-offset addressing is shown; register-offset and post-indexed forms are not modeled
The array is fixed at eight elements so the full strip stays readable

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Parallel display of index, offset, address, and instruction so the mapping between them is never hidden
keyQuestions: Why does the offset grow by four and not by one?
What does the processor do with an offset of 14?
commonMisconceptions: That the offset in the instruction is an element index
That the hardware rejects an offset past the end of an array
assessmentOpportunities: Write the VLDR instruction for element 9 of a float array at a given base
Restate the formula for an int16 array
